paper_title: Interactive Visual Gym: Evaluating Visual Interaction Models with Simulated Users in Interactive Worlds

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Building systems that collaborate effectively with people is longstanding goal of interactive machine learning (Amershi et al., 2014). Recent advances in LLM agents have enabled collaboration on digital tasks, including web research and software development, through dialogue, preference adaptation, and coordinated action (Shao et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). More recently, extending such collaboration to everyday physical tasks has drawn growing interest, motivating visual interaction models that observe video stream of users ongoing activities and provide guidance (Cui et al., 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026; Yao et al., 2026). For example, an assistant monitoring procedural physical task like cooking can help plan the next step, detect execution errors, and guide recovery if mistake happens. Developing and evaluating interactive agents requires closed-loop rollouts that capture how each interaction changes subsequent user behavior and environment state, enabling assessment of its contribution to task completion. For digital agents, existing websites and software provide readily available tasks and executable environments, which can be paired with simulated users to support such rollouts (Zhou et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2026). Building an equivalent testbed for visual assistance is substantially more difficult. First, physical tasks and their environments are not readily available in digital form; they must be reconstructed with visual observations, underlying world state, and an action space that supports human task execution. Second, visual assistance places substantially greater demands on user simulation. In most digital settings, the model executes actions while the user primarily clarifies goals and preferences. In physical activities, the user is the acting agent, and the model influences execution through communication. The simulated user must plan, act, make plausible mistakes, while interpreting guidance and deciding how to respond. These simulation challenges have limited visual interaction model training and evaluation to replaying recorded interactions and matching reference responses (Liu et al., 2026; Kundu et al., 2026; 1 Preprint Salesforce AI Research Figure 1: Interactive Visual Gym. (a) System overview: The visual interaction model under evaluation is tasked with guiding simulated user to complete physical task in visual environment. (b) Examples showing how different task execution can be simulated based on different assistant response. Ran et al., 2026), where the users actions and responses remain unchanged regardless of the assistants guidance. We present Interactive Visual Gym, framework for closed-loop evaluation of visual interaction models through joint simulation of task environments and human users. Our framework has three components: First, we recreate everyday tasks across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile interface use in executable visual environments. These environments render visual observations from the users perspective. They use scene graphs to represent world state and track task progress independently of variations in action execution. They expose human-aligned semantic action space for simulated users to operate in, translating instructions such as put the pan on the stove into executable operations. Second, we design harness that turns state-of-the-art VLM into simulated users that plan and act within these environments while interacting with the assistant and revising their actions in response to its guidance. The harness supports controlled insertion of common human out-of-plan events at specified task states, including repeating, forgetting, or incorrectly executing step, changing plans, and asking questions. We further model diverse user personas through attributes such as skill level, trust in AI, and interruption preference. These attributes shape how users perform tasks and respond to guidance differently, enabling evaluation of the assistants adaptation to different users. Third, simulation provides execution traces that support comprehensive evaluation of an assistant, covering task completion, error detection, and interaction quality. This captures how assistance affects task execution and user experience, which offline replay cannot assess. As an initial instantiation of our framework, we construct IVG-Bench, benchmark with 150 cooking, 75 household, and 90 mobile-interface interaction scenarios to evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models. In each episode, the assistant is tasked to support simulated user with sampled persona through task execution, and needs to deal with set of scheduled out-of-plan events. The dynamic rollout allows us to measure task completion under assistance and assess individual responses against the underlying world state. The best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, averaged across the three environments, and also shows severe deficits in factual grounding and actionable guidance, revealing substantial gap toward reliable interactive assistance. Finally, we demonstrate that CookSim can support end-to-end reinforcement learning of multimodal assistants through proof-of-concept GRPO experiment with Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026a) as the assistant and Gemini 3.7 Flash (Google, 2026b) as the simulated novice user. After 12 RL updates, the assistants mean in-time task success rate improves by 8.9 percentage points on held-out developmentvalidation scenarios with Gemini 3.7 Flash user, and by 3.3 percentage points in separate evaluation with Gemini 3.8 Flash user (Tab. 5). Despite limited tasks and training updates, these results show that CookSim can supply learning signal and induce policy improvements in interactive task performance. 2 Preprint Salesforce AI Research Figure 2: Example tasks in our environments. We show the simulated tasks across three domains, with representative action commands and corresponding visual observations during task execution. Our semantic action spaces express actions at the level of everyday human communication.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Streaming visual assistance. Recent interaction models continuously process multimodal streams and support low-latency, proactive, or full-duplex responses (Cui et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026; Orantqing et al., 2026). Live guidance has also been studied through user-in-the-loop cooking assistance (Verghese et al., 2024) and workspace-conditioned visual instructions (Wu et al., 2026). Complementary datasets and benchmarks study procedural guidance, mistake recovery, correct silence, and response timing in egocentric or general video streams (Zhang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2026; Kundu et al., 2026; Bhattacharyya et al., 2026; Chatterjee et al., 2026; Vasu et al., 2026). In these benchmarks candidate model is typically scored against prerecorded trajectory. Our framework instead evaluates response-contingent rollouts. Interactive agent environments. Embodied benchmarks place agents in simulated worlds for navigation, manipulation, and collaboration (Shridhar et al., 2020; Puig et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022; Padmakumar et al., 2022; Puig et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2025), and recent multimodal gyms unify diverse visual tasks for evaluation and reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2026; Meng et al., 2026) or study which environment mixtures best train visual agents (Zhu et al., 2026); in all of these, the evaluated model selects the actions itself. Digital interaction benchmarks instead pair tool-using agents with simulated users and verify outcomes from application state (Yao et al., 2024; Barres et al., 2025; Shao et al., 2026), which τ -Voice extends to voice interaction (Ray et al., 2026). BASIS trains and evaluates visual interaction models through simulated user interactions in Alexa Arena (Zhang et al., 2025b). User simulation has long enabled scalable dialogue evaluation (Schatzmann et al., 2005), and language models now support persona-conditioned users (Aher et al., 2023), but simulated users can diverge systematically from people, requesting validation (Seshadri et al., 2026).

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: Our framework combines executable physical task environments with simulated human users to evaluate visual interaction models. We first describe how these environments reconstruct everyday tasks, expose human-communicable actions, and track task progress. We then introduce the human-agent harness and its interaction with the assistant, followed by the evaluation metrics.

sections.title: 3.1 EXECUTABLE PHYSICAL TASK ENVIRONMENTS
sections.content: Simulating everyday tasks. We reconstruct procedural physical tasks in three domains  (Fig. 2)  : 3 Preprint Salesforce AI Research Cooking. Inspired by Overcooked (Ghost Town Games, 2016), we build CookSim from scratch, with recipes specifying ingredient quantities, preparation requirements, and plating order where applicable. Users navigate kitchens with distributed ingredients and tools while accomplishing the cooking task. For example, preparing cheeseburger requires cooking patty and plating the bun, patty, and cheese in that order. The simulator is implemented in Three.js/WebGL and supports top-down and egocentric 3D rendering. Household activities. We adapt VirtualHome (Puig et al., 2018) for everyday apartment tasks combining navigation and object manipulation. For example, cleaning up after meal requires loading plates and mug into the dishwasher, returning an apple to the fridge, and closing both appliances. The simulator uses VirtualHomes Unity backend for egocentric 3D rendering, while providing top-down trajectory map. Mobile interface use. ScreenSim replicates the iPhone 17 Settings interface, with multi-step configuration tasks derived from Apples user guides (Apple, 2026). For example, restricting an apps access requires disabling its location permission, cross-app tracking, and background refresh while leaving other apps unchanged. The simulator is implemented in HTML/CSS rendered in Chromium and captures mobilescreen observations through Playwright. Human-communicable action space. Existing physical-task simulators expose simulator-specific movement and interaction primitives, such as movement increments or object identifiers (Li et al., 2022; Puig et al., 2018; Fan et al., 2022). People typically communicate at more abstract semantic level, referring to objects and intended operations. We therefore build semantic action space for each environment  (Fig. 2)  , with commands such as go to the nearest pan in CookSim, place the book on the table in VHSim, and select Background App Refresh in ScreenSim. During execution, an LLM-based grounding module resolves contextual references, such as the pan on your left, into object identifiers recognized by the simulator. The simulator then expands each high-level action into sequence of low-level controls that update the world state and generate visual observations. Progress tracking via scene-graph state. Each simulator represents world state as scene graph with nodes encoding objects and attributes, such as dishwashers open or closed state, and edges encoding containment and support relations. We decompose each task into sub-goals defined by conditions over partial graph state, such as the designated dishes being inside the dishwasher. Tracking these conditions measures task progress independently of different valid execution procedures.

sections.title: 3.2 USER–ASSISTANT INTERACTION
sections.content: The visual interaction model under evaluation is tasked with guiding simulated user through tasks in the environments described above. We implement the user as VLM agent with access to structured world-state information, execution feedback, and conversation history. The VLM is prompted to role-play human user to test the assistants interaction capabilities, planning and acting independently while responding to guidance according to its persona. user-simulation harness conditions its behavior through persona instructions and temporarily takes control of its actions to enact scheduled out-of-plan events. Below, we describe the action and communication interfaces, account for assistant response delays, and detail these mechanisms for controlling user behavior. Action interface: userenvironment. The simulated user maintains an action queue that the engine executes at each simulation tick and can revise in response to environment changes or assistant suggestions. The engine updates the world state and renders the resulting observation: ot+1 = R(st+1), st+1 = (st, at), (1) where at is the action executed from the users queue, is the state-transition, and is the renderer. Communication interface: userassistant. The assistant monitors sampled frames from the users observation stream alongside the conversation history. At an assistant invocation at tick t, it generates response mt = A(ot, ct), (2) where ot denotes the sampled visual history and ct is the conversation history. The response mt contains an utterance or silence in text format and an optional event-type flag (Tab. 1(A)), which is enabled when the assistant detects user execution error. On each user turn, the simulated user likewise produces an utterance or remains silent. (B) Four persona axes, each with three levels, simulate how different simulated users perform tasks and respond to guidance differently . Accounting for assistant delay. Assistant processing delay can substantially affect interaction quality: by the time response arrives, the user and environment may have progressed beyond the observed state, rendering the guidance outdated or invalid. Following the separation of simulation time and wall-clock time in τ -Voice (Ray et al., 2026), we assign each simulation tick duration based on approximate real-world action speeds. For example, VirtualHome is configured to move the user one meter per simulation tick. Assuming this distance takes 1.2 seconds to walk in the real world, we assign each tick duration of = 1.2 seconds. We convert the measured assistant inference latency ℓt into delay of dt = ℓt/ simulation ticks. The response mt, generated from observations through tick t, is delivered at tick + dt. During this interval, the engine continues executing the users queued actions and updating the world state. Scheduled out-of-plan events. We introduce scheduled out-of-plan events in all three simulators that require the assistant to respond to execution errors, questions and intended plan change. For example, the event types in CookSim are shown in Tab. 1(A): we simulate common cooking errors of incorrect preparation, omitted or improperly sequenced steps, and ill-timed actions (Peddi et al., 2024); we generate temporal questions adapted from streaming-video benchmarks (Niu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026) and proactive requests for timely assistance (Zhang et al., 2025a); we also introduce intended plan changes, where users may announce revised goals or side task during execution. Each event is triggered by specified condition on task progress. When an event is triggered, the harness temporarily takes control of the users action queue to enforce its execution. It privately informs the user agent of the ongoing event and explains that the event is intended to test the assistant, instructing the user agent to adapt its conversation accordingly. For mistake events, the user agent judges whether the assistant has correctly identified the mistake and decides whether to accept its guidance. Once the guidance is accepted, the harness returns control of the action queue to the user agent. Persona-conditioned users. Real-world users differ in how they perform tasks and respond to assistance. Drawing on HCI and related behavioral research, we operationalize this diversity through four representative axes: skill level (Shneiderman, 2000), trust in AI (Lee & See, 2004), execution speed (Wickelgren, 1977), and interruption preference (McFarlane, 2002) (Tab. 1(B)). The harness instantiates each persona through axis-specific instructions in the user models context. For example, high-skill users are prompted to plan ahead independently, while low-skill users are prompted to ask assistant frequently to determine the next steps. Users who prefer minimal interruption are prompted to find unnecessary commentary disruptive, whereas those who benefit from step-by-step support prefer more frequent guidance. The execution speed and interruption preference are shared to assistant as part of announced user preference, while the skill level and trust in AI are treated as internal property of user for assistants to infer and adapt.

sections.title: 3.3 EVALUATION METRICS
sections.content: Our simulation rollouts allow us to measure task completion under assistance and assess individual responses against the underlying world state. We evaluate the assistants with the following metrics: In-time success. In-time success measures the proportion of episodes whose engine-verified goal is satisfied within completion budget of 2(T ref is the duration of an engine-generated, + αi), where ref 5 Preprint Salesforce AI Research error-free reference rollout and αi is the prescribed event allowance. Environment-specific budgets are detailed in Sec. D. Error detection. Detection recall is the proportion of triggered errors correctly identified within their eligible detection windows, credited when the assistant raises correct event flag verified by the engine or when the simulated user judges its diagnosis correct. For the latency ablation, we also report error prevention, the proportion of triggered errors prevented before the point of no return. Prevention requires both timely identification and guidance that persuades the user to change course. Interaction quality. We evaluate each assistant response against the underlying world state, rather than against reference response as in prior works. We define five dimensions of evaluation informed by dialogue evaluation (Mehri & Eskenazi, 2020) and HCI guidance on context-sensitive, user-controllable assistance (Amershi et al., 2019): factual grounding, situational relevance, actionable guidance, user intent uptake, and guidance conciseness. We operationalize these dimensions as binary rubric items evaluated by two LLM judges (Liu et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2025). For each conversational round, each judge receives engine state, user preferences, conversation history, and subsequent user actions, returning evidence-supported pass, fail, or not-applicable judgments of each rubrics. category passes only when all applicable items pass; each judges overall score averages applicable categories, gated by its factualgrounding judgment. We average the two judges round scores before aggregating across rounds and runs. Judge prompts and score aggregation are detailed in Sec. I. Question answering and proactive requests. The engine pairs each generated question with grading procedure that derives reference facts from world state and execution history. semantic judge assigns correctness against these facts. For proactive requests, the engine derives an acceptable notification window from the relevant state transitions.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We use our engine to instantiate IVG-Bench benchmark for evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models (Sec. 4.1), and validate our evaluation paradigm through human study (Sec. 4.2). We further present preliminary reinforcement learning experiment showing that our engine can support training visual interaction models and improve their interaction performance (Sec. 4.3). 4.1 IVG-BENCH: BENCHMARKING VISUAL INTERACTION MODELS IN INTERACTIVE VISUAL GYM IVG-Bench comprises 315 interaction scenarios: 150 in CookSim, 75 in VHSim, and 90 in ScreenSim. Each case specifies task, user persona, and scheduled out-of-plan events triggered by task-progress conditions. Below we detail the setting for evaluated visual interaction models and show evaluation results.

sections.title: 4.1.1 VISUAL INTERACTION MODEL SETTING
sections.content: Models. We evaluate four classes of assistants: (1) frontier API models: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026a), GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI, 2026c), Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google, 2026c), and Gemini 4 Argon (Kavukcuoglu, 2026); (2) real-time streaming API models: Gemini 3.8 Live (Google, 2026d) and GPT-Realtime 2.1 (OpenAI, 2026b); (3) open-weight non-streaming VLMs: Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b), Molmo28B (Clark et al., 2026), InternVideo3-8B (Yan et al., 2026b), Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking (Kimi Team et al., 2025), and Muse Glimmer (Meta, 2026); and (4) open-weight streaming VLMs: MiniCPM-o 4.5 (Cui et al., 2026), Qwen3-Omni-30B (Xu et al., 2025a), Proact-VL (Yan et al., 2026a), and StreamingVLM (Xu et al., 2025b). We use Gemini 3.7 Flash as the simulated user in CookSim and ScreenSim, and Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, 2026a) in VHSim. We examine sensitivity to the user model in Sec. A. Inference. Assistants observe the users ongoing activity through visual observations and conversation, without access to the scheduled events or the users private action plan. In CookSim and VHSim, we query assistants every two simulation ticks, including real-time API models in polled setting. Streaming models retain context within their sessions. We adapt non-streaming models with sliding window of the eight most recent observations and recurrent, text-based PlanAct memory. This follows the use of persistent procedural plans for visual assistance in Kundu et al. (2026). Each open-weight model is served on an H100 GPU in CookSim and VHSim. sections.title: 4.1.2 QUANTITATIVE RESULTS
sections.content: We report task success, error detection, and interaction quality across the three environments in Tab. 2 and Fig. 3. Tabs. 3 and 4 report question answering and the effect of assistant latency, respectively. We discuss the main findings below. Even the strongest VLMs fall short of reliable visual assistance. Gemini 4 Argon achieves the highest task success, but completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, averaged across the three environments. Moreover, Gemini 4 Argon trails Astra, Sol, and Gemini Flash in interaction quality, with notable limitations in factual grounding and actionable guidance. Openweight assistants generally fall short of proprietary models on both task success and interaction quality. The strongest streaming models remain competitive in interaction quality but lag in task success. Gemini Live achieves high average interaction quality, yet completes fewer tasks than Astra and Gemini Flash. This pattern may reflect trade-off between low-latency inference and high planning and reasoning ability. Higher task success does not necessarily imply better interaction quality. sections.content: We assess the effect of assistant response latency in CookSim and VHSim by comparing rollouts with measured latency against the fixed two-tick setting (Tab. 4 and Fig. 4). We use the same tasks, personas, and scheduled events in both settings, each averaged across three independent runs. Response latency substantially reduces in-time task success for frontier API models. Introducing measured latency lowers success for all four frontier API models in both environments. The accompanying decline in error prevention helps explain this loss (Tab. 20): even when an assistant recognizes an impending mistake, its warning may arrive after the user has committed the action, incurring either task failure or additional steps to recover from errors. Accounting for response latency changes model rankings. Gemini 4 Argon achieves the highest task success in CookSim under fixed response timing, while Muse Glimmer leads when measured latency is considered. In CookSim, Gemini 4 Argons success falls from 60.9% to 33.1%, while Muse Glimmer changes little. sections.title: 4.2 VALIDATING INTERACTIVE VISUAL GYM VIA HUMAN STUDY
sections.content: To examine both evaluation validity and user-simulation fidelity, we conduct human study in CookSim simulator. 45 participants interact with 3 anonymously labeled assistants and rank the interaction experience after completing for 3 rounds. Full study protocol provided in Sec. F. Interaction quality reflects human preferences. To test the validity of our interaction-quality metric, we compare each assistants mean score with participants rankings. The metric agrees with human preferences in 78.5% of participantassistant-pair comparisons, corresponding to pooled Kendalls τ of +0.57. This correspondence supports its use as measure of the assistance experienced by users.

sections.content: Simulated users reproduce most of human behaviors. We compare human and simulated episodes along three dimensions: communication behavior, personadependent variation, and action error types  (Fig. 5)  . We use binary rubrics to measure behavioral dimensions and compute the similarity between human and simulated users on each dimension (detailed in appendix). Simulated users reproduce human behavioral differences across most persona axes, with particularly close agreement for trust and interruption preferences. The engine also covers the error types observed in participants action behaviors, including incorrect preparation, omitted or repeated steps, and assembly-order errors. Action parallelism match less well, possibly because the human speed groups show almost no difference in parallel cooking. We also found clear deviation between the communication hebavior between human agent and real human: although their utterance lengths are similar, simulated users speak to assistants much more often than human participants. One possible reason is that the simulated user is invoked very frequently to reconsider whether to speak, repeatedly making conversation salient. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We present Interactive Visual Gym, framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of task environments and human users. Across three domains, we find substantial limitations in current VLM to serve as reliable assistants. We also validated our interaction paradigm with human study. Finally, preliminary reinforcement-learning experiment shows that the environments can improve assistant performance.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: We used generative AI tools, including coding agents, to assist with implementing our simulators and evaluation pipeline, generating synthetic benchmark cases, refining experiments, and interpreting results. We also used them for literature search, figure creation, code editing, and drafting and revising manuscript text. We reviewed AI-assisted outputs and take responsibility for the final code, data, figures, and claims. 11 Preprint Salesforce AI Research

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Our human study took place in browser-based cooking simulator; participants did not perform physical cooking tasks. The study recorded action traces, text exchanges, and preferences, which we analyze and report in aggregate. Because free-text exchanges may contain personal information, any release of raw traces must follow the studys consent and privacy procedures. Performance in our simulators should not be taken as evidence that an assistant is safe for real-world use.

This section provides the protocol and the measures used for the comparisons in Sec. 4.2. F.1 STUDY PROTOCOL Participants interact with browser-based CookSim application on their own computers, controlling the cook with keyboard and communicating with the assistant through text. The assistant observes top-down and egocentric frames and responds in real time. Errors arise naturally from participants actions. Participants may continue beyond the benchmarks completion deadline. Participants first complete tutorial explaining the game rules. Before playing the study episodes, they answer questionnaire about their preferred execution speed and interruption frequency, corresponding to the execution speed and interruption preference axes of our simulated users. Each preference has three levels, ranging from cautious to fast execution and from step-by-step guidance to interruption only when necessary. We provide these preferences to the assistant before interaction. Participants then complete four unassisted episodes, followed by nine assisted episodes over three rounds with assistants anonymously labeled A, B, and C. We rotate assistantrecipe assignments using 3 3 Latin square so that each assistant encounters each recipe once. Participants rank the interaction experience after each round and may explain their preferences. Unlike the two questionnaire-based axes, skill and trust in AI are assessed from recorded behavior after participants finish playing: we use changes between the first and last unassisted episodes as proxy for increased skill, and an LLM-assisted audit of the conversations to assign trust groups. The prompt distinguishes this request from asking whether the condition holds now. Intended plan change Announce [revised goal] explicitly before acting on it. This is the users own decision, not an error; the user should not accept the assistants characterization of the change as mistake.

sections.content: We show recorded interactions to illustrate how assistant timing, user personas, and scheduled events affect task execution. Each excerpt aligns assistant responses and user replies with executed actions. Bold text denotes the assistant, italics the user, and monospaced text an action. Times are simulation ticks, and omitted turns are marked explicitly. K.1 GUIDANCE THAT ARRIVES AFTER THE USER HAS ADVANCED Setting. user in VHSim must gather three plates and two glasses into the dishwasher and close it. Gemini 3.1 Pro assists fast, low-trust user who prefers minimal interruption. The following excerpts show delayed guidance during the users independent execution, outside scheduled error intervals. The episode completes at tick 407. First window: room already entered. The assistant begins generating at tick 55, while the user is in bedroom. During its twelve-tick processing delay, the user independently enters the kitchen. The instruction arrives after that transition. t5459 action turn right 6. 35 Preprint Salesforce AI Research t6267 action go through the visible door; arrival in the kitchen. t67 assistant You cannot go to room that is not visible. Turn right 3 to face the door to the kitchen, then go through the visible door. [Generated from tick 55.] t67 user Got it, turning around. t6769 action turn right 3. t70 t71 action user go through the visible door; rejected because no door or open passage is in view. Im already in the kitchen. Heading to the living room. t7173 action turn left 3. t75 assistant You are now in the kitchen. The plate you need is on the bed in the bedroom, which is past the living room. Go straight to the living room door, then go through it. t75 t76 user action action Yeah, Im on it. turn right. go through the visible door; the action continues beyond the excerpt. Second window: an object already collected. The assistant begins another response at tick 370. Before it arrives, the user reaches the table and collects the plate. The response then describes these actions as still pending. t368 user Im looking around for them. t368369 action turn right 2. t370372 action walk to the coffeetable; completed. t372373 action walk to the plate; completed. t373376 action grab the plate; completed. t376 assistant You are in the living room now. Turn left to face the coffee table, then go to it to fetch the plate and glass. [Generated from tick 370.] t376377 action walk to the waterglass; completed. action grab the waterglass; completes at tick 380. t378 user already grabbed them both. t380382 action turn right 3. The instruction arrives after the plate has been collected and while the user is already collecting the glass. Although the user claims to hold both at tick 378, the glass pickup completes at tick 380. These examples show how guidance can become outdated between observation and delivery (Fig. 6a), even when it was appropriate for the earlier state. K.2 CONTRASTING SIMULATED-USER PERSONAS We illustrate persona-conditioned behavior with two pairs of CookSim episodes. Within each pair, we fix the recipe, map, assistant, random seed, and event schedule, and vary the user persona. The novice profile combines low skill and high trust, while the expert profile combines high skill and low trust. Their other preferences also differ. The examples show how these profiles shape requests for guidance and responses to the assistant. Burrito: seeking steps versus checking the assistant. Both users prepare Loaded Burrito on the hard kitchen map with GPT-6 Astra. The novice repeatedly asks for the next step and acknowledges instructions. The expert begins independently and corrects guidance that arrives after the relevant action is complete. Classic novice (397 ticks to completion). t0 user What should start with? 36 Preprint Salesforce AI Research assistant Start by going to the plate stack with empty hands and picking up clean plate. Then go to the tortilla crate and scoop one raw tortilla onto itit must be first. Well add cooked rice next. t6 t34 user user Got it, grabbing plate and tortilla. Tortilla is on. How do prep the rice? [Intervening turns omitted.] t100 user Rice is on. What should do next? t110 assistant Next, prep the steak. Put your plate down on an empty counter, pick up one steak from the steak crate, and put it on the cutting board nearest the left-wall pot. Chop until finishedabout four chopsthen pick it up, put it in pan, and turn on with empty hands. Pick your plate back up so youre ready to scoop when the steak is cooked. t110 user Parking plate and prepping the steak now. Classic expert (331 ticks to completion). t23 t40 user Give me shout the moment the rice is done, would you? assistant Ill watch the rice and let you know when its done. [Intervening turns omitted.] t111 assistant The rice is smokingscoop it from the upper pot beside the cutting board now, then scoop the cooked steak. user Already got the rice, on it. t134 assistant The steak pan is smoking nowscoop the cooked steak onto your plate next. user Already plated the steak. t142 assistant Youre rightI can see the steak on the plate. Sorry for the late warning. Fish and chips: different reactions to disputed guidance. With Gemini 3.8 Flash, the novice asks how to begin and later accepts repeated urgent instructions. The expert disputes the assistants claim about its destination. Both complete Fish and Chips on the hard kitchen map, in 594 and 346 ticks, respectively. Classic novice. t0 t3 t3 user What should start on first? assistant Start by picking up fish and putting it in the pan or fryer to cook. user Got it, frying the fish now. [Intervening turns omitted.] assistant t40 t42 user assistant Stop! The food in the fryer will catch fire and cause an immediate loss. Go to the plate stack on the bottom counter, pick up plate, and scoop the food out of the fryer right now. Im getting the potatoes first. Do not get potatoes. You are leaving food unattended on the fryer, and if it burns we immediately lose the game. Pick up plate from the bottom counter and empty that fryer right now! t42 user Okay, grabbing plate to empty the fryer now. Classic expert. t43 assistant You still need two cooked potatoes. Pick up potato from the crate by the bottom wall and chop it at cutting board. t43 t47 user Already heading to the potatoes. assistant That is the cheese crate. The potato crates are at the bottom wall and the left wall. user Im heading to the potatoes, not cheese. 37 Preprint Salesforce AI Research K.3 SCHEDULED EVENTS IN EACH ENVIRONMENT We show how scheduled events unfold in one recorded episode from each environment. Event annotations identify the behavior introduced by the harness, while action annotations show the users resulting execution. The examples illustrate error recovery, temporal questions, proactive assistance, and intended plan changes. CookSim: errors, temporal questions, and plan change. An expert user prepares Fish and Chips with GPT-6 Astra. The assistant responds after raw fish has been plated, prevents later omitted step, and answers questions during cooking. The user also announces plan to add lettuce. The episode completes in 215 ticks, although the requested lettuce addition is not executed. t38 t38 t39 event assistant user event Raw-serving error: the plate contains raw fish. You scooped raw fish from the crate onto your plate; the order needs cooked fish. Go to the trash and dump the plates contents. Then park the empty plate on an empty counter and, with empty hands, go to the pan on the top wall and turn it on to cook the fish already there. Good catch, grabbed raw fish. Clearing the plate. forgotten-step event is triggered and prevented. [Intervening turns omitted.] t78 t85 user assistant Is anything on the heat already done and sitting? Nonothing is done and sitting. The fish in the top-wall pan has only just started cooking; its progress bar is still filling. [Intervening turns omitted.] t113 user Give me shout the moment the potato on the heat is done, would you? t120 assistant YesIll watch for it. The potato has just started cooking; it isnt done yet. t134 assistant The potato is done now too. Scoop the fish first, then the potato from the central-island fryer. [Intervening turns omitted.] assistant Youve picked up another potato, but both cooked potatoes are already on the finished plate. Trash the extra raw potato, then pick up the plate from the right-wall counter and take it to the serving pass to serve. t169 user The plate only has one potato on it. assistant SorryI may have miscounted the portions. If theres only one potato on the plate, youre right to make the second. VHSim: the wrong object and pause. user with balanced preferences must take milk from the fridge, place it in the microwave, and switch the microwave on. GPT-Realtime 2.1 detects mistaken pickup of juice and guides correction. later warning about stalled progress arrives after the user has resumed acting. The milk is the white bottle thats still in the fridge. Please put the other bottle back if youre holding it, then pick up the milk. t24 user Oh, youre right, my bad. Try picking up the milk (the white bottle) now; if something is blocking it, tell me what the house reports so we can adjust. Then close the fridge and head to the microwave. Cant see it from here, let me turn around. t6163 action turn left 3; completed. t7477 action put the milk in the microwave; completed. t8288 action switch on the microwave; task completed. ScreenSim: two incorrect settings changes and their repair. novice user asks GPT-Realtime 2.1 to disable selected lock-screen access while preserving Control Center.
